en jakke.explanation: "En jakke" means "a jacket". A thicker, longer one is "en frakke" (a coat). A useful phrase is "Tag en jakke med" (Take a jacket with you).

sentence.da: Tag din **jakke** på, det er koldt.
sentence.en: Put your jacket on, it is cold.

en julegave.explanation: "En julegave" means "a Christmas present". It is built from "jul" (Christmas) and "en gave" (a gift), and "at købe julegaver" means "to buy Christmas presents".

sentence.da: Jeg har købt en **julegave** til min mor.
sentence.en: I have bought a Christmas present for my mother.

et job.explanation: "Et job" means "a job" and is borrowed from English. "Et arbejde" (a job, work) means about the same. "At have et job" means "to have a job".

sentence.en: I have a new job.

et jordbær.explanation: "Et jordbær" means "a strawberry". It is made of "jord" (earth, ground) and "et bær" (a berry).

sentence.da: Om sommeren spiser vi **jordbær** med fløde.
sentence.en: In the summer we eat strawberries with cream.

et juletræ.explanation: "Et juletræ" means "a Christmas tree". It is made of "jul" (Christmas) and "et træ" (a tree).

sentence.en: We are decorating the Christmas tree today.

ja.explanation: "Ja" means "yes" and is used just like in English. "Ja, tak" means "yes, please" and is the polite way to accept an offer. If a question has "ikke" (not) in it, like "Kommer du ikke?" (Aren't you coming?), Danes answer "jo" (yes) instead of "ja".

sentence.da: **Ja**, jeg vil gerne have en kop kaffe.
sentence.en: Yes, I would like a cup of coffee.

januar.explanation: "Januar" means "January". Month names are written with a small letter in Danish, unlike in English. You can say "midt i januar" (in the middle of January) or "i begyndelsen af januar" (at the beginning of January).

sentence.en: It is cold in January.

japan.explanation: "Japan" means "Japan". It is spelled the same as in English, but said with Danish sounds. A person from Japan is "en japaner" (a Japanese person), and "japansk" means "Japanese".

sentence.en: My friend is travelling to Japan.

japansk.explanation: "Japansk" means "Japanese". It is written with a small letter in Danish, unlike "Japanese" in English. On its own it is also the name of the language: "Jeg taler japansk" (I speak Japanese). A Japanese person is "en japaner".

sentence.en: I love Japanese food.

jeg.explanation: "Jeg" means "I". Unlike English, it only has a capital letter at the start of a sentence. It sounds roughly like "yai". When something is done to you, the word is "mig" (me), as in "Han ser mig" (He sees me).

sentence.en: I live in Copenhagen.

jeg er enig.explanation: "Jeg er enig" means "I agree". Danish literally says "I am agreed" instead of using a word like "agree". To say who you agree with, add "med" (with): "Jeg er enig med dig" (I agree with you). The opposite is "uenig" (in disagreement).

sentence.en: I agree with you.

jeg er ked af det.explanation: "Jeg er ked af det" means "I'm sad", and also "I'm sorry" when you regret something. Say the whole phrase, including "af det" at the end. For a quick apology like bumping into someone, "undskyld" (sorry, excuse me) is more common; "jeg er ked af det" sounds more heartfelt.

sentence.da: **Jeg er ked af det**, men jeg kan ikke komme i dag.
sentence.en: I'm sorry, but I can't come today.

jeg forstår ikke.explanation: "Jeg forstår ikke" means "I don't understand" and is very useful when you are learning. "Forstår" means "understand" and "ikke" means "not". To say "I don't understand it", put "det" (it) before "ikke": "Jeg forstår det ikke". It goes well with "kan du gentage det?" (can you repeat that?).

sentence.en: Sorry, I don't understand.

jeg har det godt.explanation: "Jeg har det godt" means "I'm doing well" and is the usual answer to "hvordan har du det?" (how are you?). Danish literally says "I have it good", so you need "det" (it); "jeg er godt" would sound wrong. For much the same idea you can say "det går godt" (it's going well).

sentence.da: Tak, **jeg har det godt**. Og dig?
sentence.en: Thanks, I'm doing well. And you?

jeg har det skidt.explanation: "Jeg har det skidt" means "I'm not doing well" and works for feeling ill as well as feeling down. "Skidt" means "badly". A milder way to say it is "jeg har det ikke så godt" (I'm not doing so well).

sentence.da: I dag **har jeg det skidt**, fordi jeg er syg.
sentence.en: Today I'm not doing well, because I'm sick.

forms.da: Hvad hedder du? Jeg hedder Lars.

jeg hedder….explanation: "Jeg hedder…" means "my name is…" and you add your name after it. It literally means "I am called…", from "at hedde" (to be called). A common reply is "Dejligt at møde dig" (Nice to meet you).

sentence.en: My name is Anna, and you?

jeg kommer fra….explanation: "Jeg kommer fra…" means "I'm from…" and you add a country or town after it. It literally means "I come from…". It answers "Hvor kommer du fra?" (Where are you from?). For where you live now, say "jeg bor i…" (I live in…).

sentence.en: I'm from Canada.

forms.da: Jeg vil gerne have en kaffe.
Jeg vil gerne have to billetter.

jeg vil gerne have.explanation: "Jeg vil gerne have" means "I would like" and is the polite way to order or ask for something. Put the thing you want after "have". "Gerne" (gladly) makes it sound friendly; "jeg vil have" without it is blunt, like "I want".

sentence.da: **Jeg vil gerne have** en kop te.
sentence.en: I would like a cup of tea.

jer.explanation: "Jer" means "you" when you talk to more than one person and something is done to them, as in "Jeg kan se jer" (I can see you all). When they are the ones doing something, you say "I", as in "I er søde" (you are nice). For one person the word is "dig". "Jer" is also used after words like "til" (to) and "med" (with).

sentence.en: I have a gift for you (all).

jeres.explanation: "Jeres" means "your" or "yours" when you talk to more than one person, as in "jeres hus" (your house). It stays the same before any word. For one person you use "din", "dit" or "dine" (your).

sentence.en: Is that your car (you all)?

jo.explanation: "Jo" has two uses. It means "yes" when you answer a question that has "ikke" (not) in it: "Kommer du ikke?" (Aren't you coming?) "Jo!" (Yes, I am!). Inside a sentence it adds a feeling of "you know" or "of course", as in "det er jo rigtigt" (it is, you know, right). For ordinary yes answers use "ja" (yes).

sentence.da: Kan du ikke lide kaffe? **Jo**, det kan jeg.
sentence.en: Don't you like coffee? Yes, I do.

jord.explanation: "Jord" means "earth" or "soil": the soil that plants grow in, and also the ground you stand on. With a capital letter, "Jorden" is the planet Earth. For the floor inside a house Danes say "gulv" (floor), not "jord".

sentence.en: The plants grow in the soil.

juice.explanation: "Juice" means "juice". It is borrowed from English but said the Danish way. People usually say what kind it is, as in "appelsinjuice" (orange juice) or "æblejuice" (apple juice).

sentence.da: Jeg drikker et glas **juice** til morgenmad.
sentence.en: I drink a glass of juice for breakfast.

jul.explanation: "Jul" means "Christmas". You say "til jul" (at Christmas) and "i julen" (during the Christmas season), usually with no word for "a" in front. The greeting is "Glædelig jul!" (Merry Christmas!).

sentence.en: We celebrate Christmas at my grandmother's.

juleaften.explanation: "Juleaften" means "Christmas Eve", the evening of 24 December. You normally use it with no "en" (a) in front, as in "på juleaften" (on Christmas Eve).

sentence.da: Vi spiser flæskesteg hos mormor til **juleaften**.
sentence.en: We eat roast pork at grandmother's for Christmas Eve.

juli.explanation: "Juli" means "July" and is written with a small letter, unlike in English. It sounds close to "juni" (June), so check the middle: "juli" has an l and "juni" has an n.

sentence.en: Many Danes are on vacation in July.

juni.explanation: "Juni" means "June" and is written with a small letter, unlike in English. It sounds close to "juli" (July), so check the middle: "juni" has an n and "juli" has an l.

sentence.en: It stays light for a long time in June.
